hints: Look at the central atom at each angle and count the regions of electron density around it to work out its shape.
Both x and y are centred on the carbons of the $C=C$ double bond, so think about the shape around a doubly bonded carbon.
Angle z is centred on a carbon with four single bonds, so think about what the standard tetrahedral angle is.
walkthrough:
**Recall the VSEPR link between shape and angle**

Bond angle is decided by the electron pairs around the central atom. More electron domains push apart to give a characteristic shape.

Rule to use:
$$3 \text{ domains} \rightarrow \text{trigonal planar} \approx 120^\circ, \quad 4 \text{ domains} \rightarrow \text{tetrahedral} \approx 109.5^\circ$$

**Find angles x and y at the alkene**

Both x ($H-C-H$) and y ($C-C-C$) share a carbon of $C=C$. Each of those carbons has 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair, so 3 electron domains.

That gives trigonal planar geometry, so $x \approx 120^\circ$ and $y \approx 120^\circ$.

**Find angle z at the saturated carbon**

Angle z ($N-C-C$) is centred on the $C$ bonded to $NH_2$, $H$, $CH_2$ and $CO_2H$. That is four single bonds and no lone pair, so 4 electron domains.

That gives tetrahedral geometry, so $z \approx 109^\circ$. Putting it together gives $120^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $109^\circ$.

options.A: Incorrect. $90^\circ$ is the angle for octahedral geometry with 6 domains, not for the alkene carbons. Both x and y are trigonal planar and much wider than $90^\circ$.
options.B: Incorrect. While x is correctly $120^\circ$, y is wrong. Angle y is still part of the $C=C$ trigonal planar carbon, so it is about $120^\circ$, not $109^\circ$. Also z is tetrahedral, not $90^\circ$.
options.C: Correct. Well done. The two alkene carbons each have 3 electron domains and are trigonal planar, so x and y are both about $120^\circ$. The carbon for z has 4 single bonds and is tetrahedral, so z is about $109^\circ$.
options.D: Incorrect. $180^\circ$ is for linear geometry with 2 domains, such as in alkynes. Angle x is around a $C=C$ carbon with 3 domains, so it is about $120^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.
